write.desc: The reals as an ordered field: the field and order axioms and a few representative facts derived from them, absolute value and the triangle inequalities, and the inequality techniques (bounding, 'it suffices to show', the epsilon lemma) that every later epsilon proof is built from.

points.name: The field axioms
points.what: State the field axioms for addition and multiplication (associativity, commutativity, identities 0 and 1, additive and multiplicative inverses, distributivity) and see that the reals, the rationals and other systems satisfy them.

points.name: Deriving algebra from the field axioms
points.what: Prove a few familiar facts directly from the axioms, such as uniqueness of 0, 1 and inverses, 0 * a = 0, (-1)a = -a, (-a)(-b) = ab, and ab = 0 implies a = 0 or b = 0, citing an axiom at each step; and know that the rest of school algebra follows in the same way.
outside: direct proof and proof by contradiction

points.name: The order axioms and ordered fields
points.what: State the order axioms (a set of positives closed under + and * with trichotomy, or equivalently a total order compatible with + and *), define <, <=, > and >= from them, and know what an ordered field is.

points.name: Rules for inequalities from the order axioms
points.what: Prove from the axioms that a^2 >= 0, 1 > 0, inequalities can be added, multiplying by a positive keeps and by a negative reverses an inequality, 0 < a < b implies 0 < 1/b < 1/a, and 0 <= a < b implies a^2 < b^2, and use these rules confidently.

points.name: The rationals are an ordered field too
points.what: Recognise that Q satisfies every field and order axiom, so nothing so far separates R from Q and a further axiom (completeness) is needed; and see why the complex numbers cannot be made an ordered field (i^2 = -1 would have to be positive).

points.name: Absolute value and its basic properties
points.what: Define |a| by cases and prove |a| >= 0, |-a| = |a|, |ab| = |a||b|, -|a| <= a <= |a|, and |a| <= c exactly when -c <= a <= c (and the strict version), and use the last to remove absolute values from inequalities.

points.name: The triangle inequality
points.what: Prove |a + b| <= |a| + |b| from -|a| <= a <= |a|, use the variants |a - b| <= |a| + |b|, and extend it to finitely many terms |a_1 + ... + a_n| <= |a_1| + ... + |a_n|.

points.name: The reverse triangle inequality
points.what: Prove |(|a| - |b|)| <= |a - b| from the triangle inequality and use it to get lower bounds, for example to show |x| > |a|/2 when |x - a| < |a|/2.

points.name: Distance on the real line
points.what: Read |a - b| as the distance between a and b, translate |x - a| < delta into a - delta < x < a + delta as an interval around a, and use the triangle inequality for distances |a - c| <= |a - b| + |b - c|.

points.name: Chaining and bounding estimates
points.what: Build a chain of inequalities to bound a quantity, using standard moves: add and subtract a term, split with the triangle inequality, bound a numerator above and a denominator below, and replace terms by cruder but simpler bounds (for example bounding |x^2 - 4| when |x - 2| < 1).

points.name: 'It suffices to show' and working backwards
points.what: Find a proof of an inequality by working backwards from the goal to a sufficient condition in scratch work, then write the final proof forwards, checking that each step is an implication in the right direction.

points.name: Bernoulli's inequality
points.what: Prove (1 + x)^n >= 1 + nx for x >= -1 and natural n by induction, and use it as a model inequality proof and a tool for bounding powers.

points.name: The epsilon lemma: a <= b + epsilon for every epsilon
points.what: Prove that if a <= b + epsilon for every epsilon > 0 then a <= b, and that if |a - b| < epsilon for every epsilon > 0 then a = b, by contradiction with a chosen epsilon, and recognise this as the standard way to prove an inequality or equality in analysis.
outside: quantifiers 'for every' and 'there exists' and their negation

where.title: Bartle and Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis
where.detail: Section 2.1 The Algebraic and Order Properties of R (including Bernoulli's inequality and the epsilon lemma); Section 2.2 Absolute Value and the Real Line

where.title: Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis
where.detail: Section 1.2 Some Preliminaries (triangle inequality, proving a = b via |a - b| < epsilon)
